actions.body: Modern artificial intelligence architectures frequently orchestrate language models, retrievers, planners, and external tools without robust native mechanisms for self-representation or behavioral governance. System failures typically stem not only from isolated reasoning mistakes, but also from uncalibrated confidence, silent behavioral degradation, and unregulated action authority. Recent research introduces the Functional Self-Awareness Architecture, which integrates four structural components: a persistent self-model capturing system boundaries and history, uncertainty-awareness mechanisms providing reliability signals relative to declared authority, a meta-cognitive evaluation layer monitoring state independently of task execution, and self-governance interfaces enforcing constraint rules. By separating task reasoning from meta-level regulation, systems can modulate action authority stably. Summary: Multi-model AI systems can employ dedicated self-awareness and meta-cognitive layers to monitor their own operational reliability independently of standard task execution.
actions.lede: Exploring how multi-model systems implement structured self-representation and meta-cognitive evaluation to regulate operational boundaries.

Title:
A Note on Inferential Decisions, Errors and Path-Dependency
Authors:
Kangda K. Wren
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
Consider sequential binary testing under model uncertainty or misspecification in an otherwise 'ideal' setting: the a posteriori belief process and its objective conditional probability counterpart may differ but converge to the same correct outcome. We show that under common conditions (defined) unless the two are 'essentially identical', differing only by a priori factors, time-homogeneous continuous decisions based on one must fail to be path-independent with respect to state-variables based on the other or any non-essentially-identical process. The difference between them, inferential error, decomposes uniquely into two independent components: a path-independent systematic bias and a path-dependent, not necessarily systematic, error.
